LING.01.note: The Annual Review separates deliberately constructed languages from naturally changing languages, while showing that both exhibit systematic phonology, grammar, vocabulary and social use.

exercise.prompt: Create a tiny language with a sound inventory, word-order rule, plural rule and ten-word vocabulary, then describe how ordinary use could make those rules drift over generations.

LING.02.note: Leiden University's course demonstrates the comparative method through regular sound correspondences, reconstruction and the Indo-European family rather than treating Proto-Indo-European as a recorded language.

exercise.prompt: Compare a small set of cognates across three Indo-European languages, mark regular sound correspondences and propose one reconstructed ancestral form.

LING.03.note: The Ask-a-Linguist overview distinguishes linguistic determinism from weaker linguistic-relativity claims and reflects the field's rejection of the strong popular version.

article.title: The Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis
article.source: The LINGUIST List — Ask a Linguist

exercise.prompt: Take one claimed language-thought effect and separate vocabulary availability, attention, memory, categorisation, cultural practice and the stronger claim that thought is impossible without a word.

LING.04.note: The Unicode Standard surveys alphabetic, abjad, syllabic, abugida and logographic systems through the practical problem of representing their characters digitally.

exercise.prompt: Classify twelve scripts as alphabet, abjad, abugida, syllabary, logography or mixed system, and state what linguistic unit each basic sign represents.

LING.05.note: Stanford's entry presents the evidence and arguments around innate language capacity while distinguishing broad biological preparedness from specific Universal Grammar proposals.

exercise.prompt: Build the strongest poverty-of-the-stimulus argument you can, then list alternative explanations based on statistical learning, cognition, interaction and cultural evolution.

LING.06.note: The Annual Review explains current debates about pidgin and creole formation, contact ecologies and the problems with treating all creoles as one exceptional language type.

article.title: Pidgins and Creoles: Debates and Issues

exercise.prompt: Compare a pidgin and a creole by social history, native-speaker status, vocabulary sources, grammar and community identity without assuming a universal one-generation pathway.

LING.07.note: UNESCO frames language revitalisation as community-led work involving education, intergenerational transmission, documentation, technology, public services and language rights.

exercise.prompt: Design a ten-year revitalisation plan covering fluent elders, children, teacher training, orthography, media, public domains, digital tools and community ownership.

LING.08.note: The British Museum explains the decree's three scripts and how comparison, earlier work and Champollion's insight made Egyptian hieroglyphs readable again.

article.title: Everything You Ever Wanted to Know About the Rosetta Stone

exercise.prompt: Explain why a trilingual inscription helps decipherment, then distinguish identifying proper names from proving the phonetic and grammatical values of an entire script.

LING.09.note: The open linguistics textbook classifies widening, narrowing, amelioration, pejoration, metaphor and metonymy as recurring pathways of semantic change.

exercise.prompt: Research five words whose meanings changed and classify each change as widening, narrowing, amelioration, pejoration, metaphor, metonymy or another documented pathway.

LING.10.note: The International Phonetic Association's official chart maps consonants, vowels, suprasegmentals and diacritics to articulatory categories and standard symbols.

exercise.prompt: Transcribe ten words from your own accent, labelling each consonant by place, manner and voicing and each vowel by height, backness and rounding.

LING.11.note: The paper begins from the linguistic fact that signed languages are natural human languages with their own phonology, morphology, syntax and communities, not encoded spoken language.

article.title: Including Signed Languages in Natural Language Processing
article.source: Julie A. Hochgesang et al. — arXiv

exercise.prompt: Compare one signed and one spoken language across phonological units, word formation, syntax, discourse, regional variation and the role of physical modality.

LING.12.note: Stanford's treatment of translating Chinese philosophy shows how lexical range, grammar, historical concepts and philosophical commitments make translation an interpretive argument rather than word substitution.

exercise.prompt: Compare three translations of one short passage, identify where wording encodes interpretation, and write an annotated translation explaining each unavoidable trade-off.
